newsitem.title: USA: US Senate panel refuses to set aside aid for Egypt. [CORRECTED 4:04 GMT]
newsitem.headline: US Senate panel refuses to set aside aid for Egypt. [CORRECTED 4:04 GMT]

text.p: Intending to send a message of displeasure for Egypt's "emerging ties" with Libya, a U.S. Senate subcommittee on Wednesday agreed to a foreign aid package with no money set aside for the Cairo government.

For the first time since Egypt and Israel signed the U.S.-brokered Camp David peace accords of 1978 (Corrects from 1979), of the two signatories only Israel would be assured of a share in the annual U.S. foreign aid budget.

The Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Foreign Operations agreed to provide $3.0 billion for economic and military assistance to Israel and set nothing aside for Egypt. Last year Egypt had received $2.1 billion.

The effort runs counter to the Clinton administration's policy and so would not necessarily mean a cut off of aid. The State Department would be free to provide aid to Cairo from the rest of the U.S. foreign aid budget.

"The emerging military, economic and political ties to Quadafi (Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi) reflect Egypt's shift from a partner in peace to an advocate for a terrorist state armed with chemical weapons," subcommittee chairman Mitch McConnell, a Kentucky Republican, said.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak Friday ended a visit to Libya with a package of deals including a yearly target of $1 billion for their trade exchanges and a free trade zone accord.

At the same time, Egypt has stepped up diplomatic activity to try to advance the stalled Israeli-Palestinian peace talks. Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa left Cairo for Rome on Wednesday on a mission to muster European support for the talks.
And Mubarak's senior political adviser Osama al-Baz was to leave on Thursday for Israel and the Palestinian self-rule areas for another round of shuttle diplomacy with leaders of both sides.

McConnell noted that progress has been made in the years since Camp David, but emphasised that in the decisions on this year's foreign aid Egypt's role in the Middle East peace process was regarded as having changed "significantly."

McConnell charged in a statement that Mubarak had undercut the Hebron negotiations and took the lead in suspending multilateral peace talks. "He convened the Arab League in Cairo where there was a vote to reimpose the economic boycott of Israel," he said.
"President Mubarak was the only leader who rejected President Clinton's summit call last September," he said.
"And, of most alarm, is the effort to cosy up to Libya," he said.

Since the Camp David accords, Egypt has received over $42 billion in U.S. foreign assistance and Israel over $59 billion. With the decline in annual U.S. spending on foreign aid since the mid-1980's, Egypt and Israel have received the lion's share.
The subcommittee approved a total foreign aid budget of $13.2 billion, only slightly below President Clinton's request and $800 million above fiscal 1997 funding.

This is the first step in congressional debate on the fiscal 1998 foreign aid appropriations. The subcommittee's plan is to go before the full Appropriations Committee this month before reaching the full Senate. It also has not yet been considered by the House spending committees.
